title: Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa
hook: on the climb to Sabarimala, every stranger on the path is called swami

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa: the impossible cure, and the boy who came home riding a tigress. Did a thankless task bring anything back? Today, the last of our Kerala days. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-nine.

Swami. A man in a black dhoti says it to the tea seller at the bottom of the hill. The tea seller says it back. A pilgrim with gray hair says it to a teenager who's stopped to catch his breath, and the teenager says it to him. On the forest path up to Sabarimala, it's how people greet each other, thank each other, ask each other to move aside. Swami, the word for a master, a holy one, the Lord, used for everyone. Today, the pilgrimage up Ayyappa's hill, and the name every pilgrim shares.
screen: `SWAMI, SAID TO EVERYONE` → `A FOREST PATH UP A HILL` → `THE NAME EVERY PILGRIM SHARES`

segments.voice: First, the shrine. Tradition says that when Manikandan's work on earth was done, he shot an arrow, and asked that his temple be built where it fell. It fell on a hill in the forest: Sabarimala, where Ayyappa is worshiped seated in meditation. Second, the vow. Pilgrims don't just set out. For a season before the climb they keep a vow. They wear a bead necklace, dress in black or dark blue, eat simple food, give up alcohol and keep celibacy, and often walk barefoot. From the day the necklace goes on, the pilgrim is called swami, and even Ayyappa, by name. The vow makes the pilgrim a little like the god they're going to see. Third, the bundle. Each pilgrim climbs with the irumudi on the head, a cloth bundle tied in two parts. One part carries offerings, including a coconut filled with ghee for the god. The other carries food for the road. On the way up, the forest echoes with a chant: Swamiye saranam Ayyappa, Lord, you are my refuge, Ayyappa. And on the way, pilgrims stop at Erumeli, where Ayyappa's companion in the stories, a Muslim named Vavar, is honored too. Now put it together. Rich and poor, old and young, wear the same dark cloth, carry the same bundle, and answer to the same name. Tradition says that above the shrine are the words tat tvam asi, that thou art, from the Upanishads. Some hear it as the god speaking to the pilgrim: what you came looking for, you are. That's where Kerala leaves us: a king welcomed home with flowers, and a hill where every stranger is swami. What would change if you greeted people as if something holy were in them?
screen: `WHERE THE ARROW FELL` · `A SEASON OF VOWS` · `THE IRUMUDI ON THE HEAD` · `THAT THOU ART`

segments.voice: A climb, with a chant. Sit up as if you were standing at the foot of a hill. Breathe in slowly, and on each out-breath, take one step up in your mind. Notice the people beside you on the path. Each time a face comes to mind, someone easy or someone hard, greet them inwardly the pilgrim's way: swami. If you pray, you can say the pilgrims' chant, Swamiye saranam Ayyappa, softly, in time with the steps. The bell holds the time.
Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa. Today, the pilgrimage to Sabarimala: the vow, the two-part bundle, the chant, and every pilgrim called swami. Today's word.
Your line: Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa. Today, treat one stranger the way pilgrims on the hill treat each other: as someone worth a holy name. Day one thousand three hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Pilgrims to Sabarimala keep a season of vows, wearing a bead necklace and dark clothes and calling one another swami, then climb the hill carrying the irumudi bundle on their heads, chanting Swamiye saranam Ayyappa.
